Plastics are a heat problem, not a strength problem: acrylic (Plexiglas) melts and re-welds behind the blade or chips and cracks if attacked fast; use a fine or plastic-specific blade, slow speed, zero orbit, gentle feed, and leave protective film on; if the kerf melts closed, slow down further — some workers run a bead of water or cut sandwiched between sacrificial hardboard. PVC pipe and trim cut easily at low speed. Non-ferrous metals — aluminum sheet, plate, and profiles, brass, copper — want 12 to 24 TPI metal blades depending on thickness, slow speed, zero orbit, and a drop of cutting oil or even candle wax on the blade; aluminum loads gullets, so clear chips often. Steel sheet up to a few millimeters is a legitimate jigsaw job with a 21 to 24 TPI bi-metal blade, lowest speed, zero orbit, oil, and patience — expect slow progress and a hot workpiece; thin sheet under about one millimeter should be sandwiched between plywood or hardboard scraps so the teeth always have three in contact and the sheet cannot chatter and tear. Ceramic wall tile (not dense porcelain) yields to a carbide-grit blade at low speed with water sponged on to cool and suppress dust; cuts are slow and edges need rubbing smooth. Fiber-cement siding demands a carbide blade, extraction, and a proper respirator because its dust contains crystalline silica. Two universal habits close the table: let the blade reach full speed before touching the work, and let the saw finish the stroke fully before withdrawing from an incomplete kerf, or the snagging blade will kick the workpiece and bend or break.

sections.heading: Setting Up: Saw, Blade, and a Kit That Covers Most Jobs
sections.body: Five minutes of setup prevents most jigsaw failures, and the routine is always the same. Unplug the saw or remove its battery before touching the blade — reciprocating tools have no forgiving direction. Fit the right blade for the material and confirm it clicks home fully in the clamp and seats in the groove of the guide roller behind it; a blade riding outside the roller will cut bevels you did not ask for. Sight down the blade from the front: it should stand square to the shoe, and if a previous job bent it even slightly, discard it — a bent blade cannot cut straight and costs less than the wood it ruins. Check the shoe: locked at exactly zero for square cuts (verify occasionally with a small square against the blade, because bevel locks drift), the anti-splinter insert fitted for fine face work, the plastic overshoe on for scratch-prone surfaces, off for maximum stability on rough ones. Set orbit and speed for the material, connect dust extraction if the saw has a port or switch on the blower so the line stays visible, and put on safety glasses — a jigsaw throws chips upward, directly toward the face, and hearing protection is sensible for any extended session. Then check the path under the cut: the blade projects below the work by the stroke length plus spare blade, and it will happily saw into the sawhorse, the cable, or the second layer of the sheet; drape the cord over a shoulder or use a cordless saw, and confirm nothing but air sits beneath the line. A modest kit covers nearly every household job, and it is worth assembling once rather than improvising each time. The essentials the text that follows assumes are listed here, and none is exotic: all are stocked by any hardware store or online tool retailer, and the total cost is small compared to a single cabinet-grade sheet of plywood.
ingredients: A jigsaw with variable speed, orbital settings, tool-less T-shank clamp, and a tilting shoe; cordless is convenient, corded is fine

Assorted T-shank blades: coarse 6 TPI wood, general 10 TPI wood, fine-finish ground 10-12 TPI, scroll blades for tight curves, 21-24 TPI bi-metal for metal, reverse-tooth for laminate, carbide-grit for tile or cement board
Two quick-grip clamps and two G-clamps or screw clamps for workholding
A pair of sawhorses or a portable workbench, plus rigid foam insulation board as a full-sheet cutting bed
Marking tools: sharp pencils, a fine marker for dark or rough stock, a utility knife for scoring veneers, masking tape
Layout tools: combination square, tape measure, a compass or improvised string-and-pencil trammel, a flexible batten or thin strip for fair curves
A drill with twist and spade bits (6-12 mm) for starter holes in interior cutouts
Safety kit: safety glasses, hearing protection, a dust mask or respirator rated for fine dust, and dust extraction or a shop vacuum where possible
Cutting lubricant for metal (cutting oil, or a wax candle rubbed on the blade), and abrasives, files, and a sanding block for edge cleanup

sections.heading: Workholding: Clamping and Supporting the Cut
sections.body: More jigsaw problems trace to the workpiece than to the saw. The blade cuts on the upstroke, pulling the work up toward the shoe and dropping it again up to fifty times a second; if the piece can move, it will chatter, the kerf will hammer itself wide, the edge will splinter, and blades will snap. The first principle is therefore rigidity: clamp the work to something heavy, with the cut line overhanging the support by only a modest amount — close enough to the support that the piece cannot flex, far enough that the blade clears the bench. Two clamps beat one, because a single clamp is a pivot. Pad clamp jaws with scrap or cork against finished surfaces. The second principle is managing the offcut. A falling offcut tears a splintered spelch out of the last few centimeters of an otherwise clean cut and can pinch the blade as it sags; support both sides of the line for anything heavy, or have a helper cradle (not pull) the waste, or leave a few millimeters uncut at the end and finish with a handsaw where the piece truly cannot be supported. For long cuts in sheet goods, the elegant solution is to abandon sawhorses-as-bridges entirely and lay the whole sheet flat on a sacrificial bed: a slab of rigid foam insulation 25 to 50 millimeters thick on the floor or across a bench supports the panel continuously on both sides of the kerf, the blade harmlessly scores the foam, nothing sags, nothing pinches, and the cut edge stays clean end to end. The same trick in miniature — a piece of sacrificial hardboard or plywood clamped under the work — both supports thin or flexible stock and nearly eliminates bottom-face breakout, because the fibers at the exit of each tooth are backed by material. Thin sheet metal must be sandwiched top and bottom this way or it will shriek, chatter, and tear. Small workpieces deserve special caution: never hold a small piece in one hand and saw with the other; clamp it, or clamp it inside a larger scrap with a V-notch cut to cradle it. Cutting installed work — countertops, floorboards, door bottoms, wall paneling — inverts the problem: the work is rigid but the surroundings are vulnerable, so check what the blade will meet below (pipes, cables, joists), choose blade length so the stroke's bottom clears anything critical, and where a floorboard must be cut over empty joist space, angle a shallow-set circular saw or use a short blade and keep the shoe flat. Finally, sawing generates a surprising sideways push in curves as the blade's back bears against the kerf wall; a well-clamped piece absorbs this invisibly, while a loosely held one skates — which the beginner then corrects with steering, compounding wander. Rigid work, supported offcut, clear underside: with those three conditions met, an inexpensive saw cuts like an expensive one.

sections.heading: Layout: Marking Curves That Deserve to Be Cut
sections.body: A cut can only be as good as its line, and curve layout is a small craft of its own. For circles and arcs, the compass family does the work: a pencil compass to about 150 millimeters radius, and beyond that a trammel — any rigid strip with a nail or awl through one end as the pivot and a pencil through a hole at the radius. A string looped from a center nail to a pencil works at any size but stretches; keep the string taut and the pencil vertical, and accept that a wooden trammel is more faithful. Mark the center on tape if the surface must stay unmarred. For ellipses, the gardener's method — two pins at the foci with a slack string loop around them and the pencil — draws a true ellipse once the foci are found (each focus lies along the long axis at a distance from the center equal to the square root of half-the-long-axis squared minus half-the-short-axis squared); for a quick approximation, many workers simply trace a large round object of pleasing size. Free curves — the sweep of a shelf bracket, the fair line of a boat frame or a garden-bed edge — are drawn with a batten: a thin, straight-grained strip of wood or a length of PVC trim bent through the points the curve must pass, held by clamps, nails, or a helper's fingers, and traced. The batten's own stiffness distributes curvature evenly and produces what boatbuilders call a fair curve, one with no sudden changes the eye or the saw will stumble over; sight along any drawn curve from a low angle and unfair bumps jump out for correction before cutting. Repeated or precious shapes deserve a template: draw and cut the shape once in hardboard or 6-millimeter MDF, refine it with files and sandpaper until perfect, then trace around it for every copy — and if perfection matters, jigsaw each copy a couple of millimeters outside the traced line and finish with a router and flush-trim bearing bit running on the template, which yields identical, polished edges the jigsaw alone cannot. Scribing fits a workpiece to an irregular surface such as a wavy wall: set a compass to the widest gap between wall and piece, ride the point down the wall while the pencil transfers every bump onto the piece, and cut to the scribed line with a slight back-bevel so the visible edge touches first. Practical marking matters as much as geometry: use a sharp pencil (a knife line for veneered faces, since the severed fibers then release cleanly), mark on masking tape on dark, rough, or melamine surfaces where graphite vanishes, and always mark the waste side with hatching — half the ruined workpieces in the world were cut accurately on the wrong side of a correct line. Decide the blade's relationship to the line before starting: cut just on the waste side, leaving the line intact, so the final dimension survives sanding. The line is a contract; layout is where the job is really decided.

sections.heading: Straight and Guided Cuts
sections.body: Curves are the jigsaw's specialty, but every project mixes in straight cuts, and they expose the tool's flexible-blade nature most cruelly, so technique matters. Freehand, the method is the same relaxed discipline as steering a car: stand or kneel so the forearm can travel the full cut without re-planting, grip lightly, keep the shoe flat and fully on the work, look at the line a few centimeters ahead of the blade rather than at the blade itself, and feed only as fast as the blade cuts willingly. Forcing is the cardinal sin — push harder than the teeth can chew and the flexible blade bows backward and sideways, the cut bellies out of square in the thickness (perfect on top, drifting below), and the extra friction burns the edge. If the saw slows or the motor labors, ease off; if the cut still crawls, the blade is wrong or dull, and no amount of muscle fixes either. A blade that constantly pulls to one side has uneven set or a bent body and belongs in the bin. For long straight cuts, guides remove steering entirely. The manufacturer's rip fence, a T-shaped rod through the shoe, rides a factory edge at up to 20 centimeters or so. Better and more general is a clamped straightedge — a spirit level, a factory plywood strip, or a purpose-made guide rail — set back from the line by the offset between the blade and the edge of the shoe. Measure that offset once with a rule (blade side to shoe edge, typically 35 to 40 millimeters, and note it is different on each side of the shoe), mark it on the saw, and clamping guides becomes a thirty-second habit; keep the shoe pressed lightly against the guide throughout, since drifting away ruins the cut as surely as no guide at all. Some shoes accept adapters for circular-saw guide-rail systems, worth using if already owned. Even guided, a jigsaw's long straight cut in thick stock will show slight under-bevel where the free blade end lags in dense grain; where a dead-square thick edge matters, cut a millimeter or two proud and plane or rout to the line, or use a circular saw for the straights and reserve the jigsaw for the curves — using each tool for its strength is not defeat but craft. Circles deserve a mention here because they are straight-line cutting's rotary cousin: the same rip-fence rod on most saws converts to a circle-cutting trammel with a pivot point, swinging the saw around a center pin for wheels, speaker holes, and round tabletops up to the rod's reach; start the cut from a drilled hole inside the waste, spiral gently out to the circumference, then let the trammel take over. Cut a test circle in scrap first — pivot play shows up as a visible lump where the cut closes on its start.

sections.heading: Cutting Curves: Steering, Feed, and Reading the Blade
sections.body: Curve cutting is a conversation between hands and blade, and the grammar can be stated plainly. Set zero orbit — orbital action widens the effective kerf front-to-back and makes the blade fight turns — and choose the narrowest blade the material allows: a standard wood blade sweeps gentle curves happily, but tight work wants a scroll blade, whose narrowed body turns in roughly half the radius. Position the body so the whole curve can be cut in one flowing pass without re-gripping; where that is impossible, plan pause points on the gentlest parts of the line, never mid-turn. Start the saw at full speed, enter the cut, and steer the way a boat is steered: the saw rotates around the blade, so turning is a smooth swing of the tool's tail while the blade itself advances along the line, and the shoe stays flat and planted through every degree of the turn. The two beginner errors are opposites of each other. The first is steering with side pressure — pushing the blade sideways toward the line like a pencil — which flexes the free bottom end of the blade so the top of the cut follows the line while the bottom undercuts wide; the cut looks right until the pieces separate and the edge is beveled and bellied. The correction is always rotation, never lateral push. The second is feeding too fast for the turn: a blade can only remove so much material per stroke, and in a curve it must remove extra from the kerf's outer wall; rushing makes the blade twist, wander, and overheat. Slow the feed in the turns and let the speed live in the straights, exactly like driving. Watch the line, not the blade — specifically, watch where the line disappears under the front of the shoe a few centimeters ahead, and keep the sawdust blown or extracted off it, because a steering correction made late is a visible flat spot on the finished curve. If the blade begins to sing, smoke, or lag, retreat: back the saw up a few millimeters within the kerf while running (never while stopped, and never yank a stalled blade sideways out of a cut), then resume at a gentler feed. When a cut must change direction sharply and the radius is beyond the blade's ability, do not force the turn; run out into the waste, loop around, and come back at the line from the new direction, or use relief cuts. Two habits produce visibly better curves immediately. First, cut fractionally on the waste side and treat the last half millimeter as sanding allowance — a curve smoothed with a sanding block, drum, or spokeshave forgives every tiny wobble the saw left. Second, practice the specific curve on scrap of the same material for thirty seconds; hands learn a radius astonishingly fast, and the scrap teaches the exact feed rate at which this blade in this wood cuts sweetly. Fluency at curves is nothing more than these rules made automatic.

sections.heading: Tight Radii, Relief Cuts, and Sharp Corners
sections.body: Every blade has a minimum turning radius set by its width from tooth tip to back edge — force a tighter turn and the blade twists in the kerf, binds, burns, and either wanders off line or snaps. A standard wood blade around 7 to 8 millimeters wide turns comfortably down to roughly 25 to 40 millimeters of radius; a scroll blade around 4 millimeters wide manages 10 to 15; nothing hand-held turns a true zero. The craft lies in strategies that make tight geometry cuttable anyway. Relief cuts are the master technique for tight outside curves: before cutting the curve itself, make a series of straight cuts from the waste edge inward, stopping just shy of the line, spaced a couple of centimeters apart around the tight section. As the curve cut then proceeds, each waste segment falls away in turn, the kerf stays open behind the blade, and the blade negotiates the curve as a series of gentle arcs instead of one impossible turn. The tighter the radius, the closer the relief cuts. For tight inside curves, drill instead: bore a hole with a twist or Forstner bit whose radius equals the desired corner radius, placed tangent to both lines inside the waste, then saw along each line into the hole — the drilled arc becomes the finished corner, cleaner than any steered turn, and a row of such holes can pre-form an entire serpentine line. For sharp interior corners, as in a rectangular cutout, the honest geometry is that a round blade path cannot produce a square inside corner directly; the standard sequence is to saw the first side past the corner slightly into the waste, loop out through the waste and back to cut the second side cleanly into the corner, then return to nibble out the remaining fillet with the blade's front teeth, or simply finish the last few millimeters of each corner with a handsaw, chisel, or rasp. Where the corner will be visible and crisp matters, drill a small hole at each corner first (inside the waste, tangent to both lines), saw hole to hole, and square the corners by hand — and remember that in many materials a small radiused corner is structurally better than a sharp one, because square inside corners concentrate stress and start cracks, which is why aircraft windows are round; specify a radius wherever the design allows. On-the-spot direction changes have a technique of their own: to turn the saw around inside a cut without a loop, cut forward, back the blade up a couple of centimeters, and re-cut while swinging gently, widening the kerf enough locally for the blade to rotate — slower than looping through waste, but invaluable when the waste is not expendable. Finally, spiral-toothed scroll blades that cut in any direction exist for extreme pattern work, at real cost in edge quality and control; for most users, relief cuts, drilled corners, and waste loops cover everything a pattern can demand.

sections.heading: Interior Cutouts: Sink Openings, Slots, and Windows
sections.body: The interior cutout — a hole that starts and ends inside a panel, touching no edge — is the jigsaw's defining job, and the sink opening in a kitchen worktop is its classic exam. The universal method is the drilled starter hole: bore 10 to 12 millimeter holes in the waste, snug against but not touching the line, drop the blade in, and saw away; a hole near each corner of a rectangular opening means the corners nearly cut themselves. The alternative is the plunge cut, for experienced hands only: with a short, stiff blade at zero orbit, tip the saw forward onto the front edge of its shoe over open waste, start at full speed, and pivot slowly down so the moving teeth mill their own entry slot until the shoe lies flat. It saves drilling in soft sheet materials and goes wrong suddenly if rushed — practicing on scrap, or simply drilling, is never wrong. For a sink or hob, lay out from the manufacturer's template or the measured rim: the cut line falls inside the rim by the specified flange width (commonly around 10 millimeters), corners get their radius, and everything is checked against the actual appliance and the cabinet below — including rails, pipes, and cables in the blade's path. Laminate tops chip: use a reverse-tooth blade from above, or tape and knife-score the line. What ruins most openings is the unsupported waste, which sags near the end, pinches the blade, and tears the final corner — so support it before the last side. The numbered procedure below is worth following literally the first several times; slots and windows in paneling follow the same logic scaled down, with one addition for walls: check behind with a stud finder and live-wire detector before cutting any surface you cannot see behind.
steps: Mark the opening from the template or the measured appliance rim, checking the flange overlap on all sides and the clearance inside the cabinet below.
Confirm the underside of the cut path is clear of rails, pipes, and cables, and set blade length so the stroke bottom clears anything close.
Tape the line on laminate or veneer, re-mark on the tape, and score the surface layer with a sharp knife.
Drill a 10-12 mm starter hole in the waste near each corner, just clear of the line, keeping the drill vertical.
Fit the right blade (reverse-tooth for laminate from above, fine ground for veneer), set zero orbit and medium speed, and fit the anti-splinter insert.
Insert the blade in a starter hole, let it reach full speed, and cut each side just on the waste side of the line, corner hole to corner hole.
Before cutting the final side, support the waste: screw a batten across it onto the waste, or station a helper below to cradle it without pulling.
Complete the final side at a gentle feed, lift out the waste, and finish corners to their radius with a rasp or sanding drum.
Test-fit the appliance, ease the opening where it binds, then seal exposed chipboard or wood edges (silicone or sealer) before final installation.

sections.heading: Bevel Cuts and Cutting at an Angle
sections.body: Every jigsaw shoe tilts, and the bevel capability is more useful than most owners realize, but it obeys stricter physics than square cutting. Mechanically, a lever or a hex-key screw releases the shoe, which pivots to detents commonly at 15, 30, and 45 degrees and locks anywhere between; detents are convenient but not gospel, so for work that matters, set the angle with a protractor or a sliding bevel against the blade itself, and cut a test piece — shoe scales on inexpensive saws are routinely a degree or two off, and a degree matters when two beveled edges must meet. The uses are everywhere once noticed. A 45-degree bevel lets skirting boards, trim, and boxes meet at mitered corners. A slight back-bevel of 3 to 5 degrees is the secret of scribed fitting: when a cabinet side or worktop is scribed to a wavy wall, back-beveling the cut means only the visible top edge touches the wall, so it can be eased with a plane or sander to a perfect line without removing material across the whole thickness. Beveled curves — a rounded worktop end with an under-bevel, a decorative arch with a chamfered face — are a jigsaw specialty no circular saw can copy. The physics that changes with tilt: the blade now crosses the material diagonally, so the effective thickness it must cut grows (at 45 degrees, by a factor of about 1.4), feed must slow accordingly, and blade length must be rechecked, since a blade that cleared the work square may bottom out or leave teeth buried on the diagonal. The flexible blade's tendency to deflect grows too — cutting force now has a component pulling the shoe sideways across the work — so bevel cuts want a firm grip on the shoe, zero or low orbit, a stiffer, wider blade than the same cut square, and ideally a clamped guide for straight bevels, because correcting a wandering bevel mid-cut is nearly impossible without leaving a visible step. Splinter behavior shifts as well: the acute-angle face of the cut (the undercut side) is delicate and prone to breakout, so orient the work to put the acute edge where it will be hidden, or tape and score it. Compound situations — a bevel along a curve — are cut exactly like any curve but slower still, and it pays to rehearse on scrap because the visual alignment of blade to line changes with tilt and the eye needs a minute to recalibrate. Two cautions complete the picture: always re-square and verify the shoe at zero afterward, since a shoe left at two degrees quietly ruins the next week of square cuts, and never tilt so far that the blade's stroke can strike the shoe or the roller — check by hand-cycling with the tool unplugged after any large angle change.

sections.heading: Beyond Wood: Metal, Plastics, Laminate, and Tile
sections.body: The jigsaw's second career as a universal sheet-cutting tool depends entirely on respecting each material's failure mode. Metal fails by heat and vibration. In steel sheet — brackets, panels, auto bodywork up to roughly 3 millimeters — use a 21 to 24 TPI bi-metal blade, the lowest speed the saw offers, zero orbit, and lubrication: proper cutting oil, or the workshop standby of rubbing a wax candle along the blade, renewed as it cuts. Progress is measured in millimeters per second, the swarf and the work get genuinely hot (gloves for handling afterward, and keep sawdust cleared away since hot chips can smolder in it), and the reward for patience is a controlled curve in steel that tin snips would distort. Thicker steel, above about 5 or 6 millimeters, is technically possible with the right blade and endless patience but is honestly better work for an angle grinder, bandsaw, or reciprocating saw. Aluminum and other non-ferrous metals cut faster with a slightly coarser metal blade around 12 to 17 TPI, but aluminum's soft chips weld into the gullets — lubricate generously and clear the blade often. All thin sheet under about a millimeter demands the sandwich: clamp it between two pieces of scrap plywood or hardboard and cut the whole stack, which keeps three teeth engaged, silences the chatter, and leaves both faces clean. Plastics fail by heat in a different way: acrylic melts around 160 degrees Celsius and either welds itself shut behind the blade or, cut too aggressively, cracks and chips; polycarbonate is tougher but gums. Use a fine or plastic-rated blade, low speed, zero orbit, light feed, leave any protective film on, back the cut with scrap, and if the kerf re-fuses, slow the stroke rate further — melted-shut cuts are a speed problem, never a blade-sharpness problem. PVC, ABS, and composite decking cut like agreeable softwood at low-to-medium speed. Laminates and melamine-faced boards fail by chipping at the brittle surface: the full defensive stack is a clean-cut or reverse-tooth blade, zero orbit, taped and knife-scored line, anti-splinter insert, and the good face oriented away from the tooth exit (down for standard blades, up for reverse-tooth). Ceramic wall tile — the softer, red- or white-bodied kind — cuts on a carbide-grit blade at low speed with water sponged into the kerf, enabling the curved cuts around pipes and toilet flanges that tile nippers butcher; dense porcelain and stone defeat the method and belong to diamond blades in a wet saw or grinder. Fiber-cement board cuts with dedicated carbide blades but liberates crystalline silica dust, a serious lung hazard: cut outdoors with extraction and a properly fitted P2/N95 or better respirator, or score-and-snap instead. Plaster, drywall, and insulation boards cut easily with coarse blades but reward a knife-and-snap where straightness suffices. In every material the diagnostic loop is identical: listen and watch — squeal means speed or pressure, chatter means support, smoke means blade or feed — and change the variable, not the effort.

sections.heading: From Saw Cut to Finished Edge
sections.body: A jigsaw cut is a beginning, and the difference between amateur and professional work is mostly what happens in the ten minutes after the saw stops. Plan for finishing before cutting: stay a hair on the waste side of the line, leaving half a millimeter to a millimeter of material as a fairing allowance, because it is easy to remove wood and impossible to reattach it. For convex curves, a sanding block wrapped in 80- then 120- then 180-grit paper, worked along (not across) the curve with long strokes, erases saw marks and small wobbles together; keep the block moving through the whole sweep so no one spot dishes. Concave curves want a round form — a sanding drum in a drill or drill press is the fast answer, and a dowel or a spray can wrapped in abrasive is the manual one; match the form's radius to or below the curve's so it rides the surface fairly. Rasps and files bridge saw and abrasive where more than a millimeter must go: a half-round rasp hogs wood quickly (cutting on the push stroke, lifted on the return), a file refines, and the modern milled-tooth rasps cut fast and clog little. A spokeshave — the curve specialist's plane — produces the fairest edges of all in skilled hands, reading the grain and shaving downhill. Check fairness by eye and hand constantly: sight along the curve from a low angle for lumps, and run fingertips along it — skin detects a 0.1-millimeter step that eyes miss. For edges that must be perfect or repeated, the router and flush-trim bearing bit remain the gold standard: fix the refined template to the work, let the bearing ride the template, and the bit machines the sawn edge into an exact copy, glassy and identical every time; climb-cut gingerly where grain tears. Square the arrises (the corners between edge and face) intentionally — a light chamfer or a pass of 120-grit at 45 degrees prevents splintering in use and looks deliberate. Tearout repair, when prevention failed: shallow top-face splinters usually vanish into a small chamfer or roundover; deeper chips glue back if the splinter survived (CA glue, tape clamp, sand flush) or fill with matching wood filler under paint. Sealed edges matter in kitchens and baths — chipboard and MDF drink water through cut edges and swell irreversibly, so any cutout near moisture gets its raw edge coated with silicone, PVA sealer, or paint before installation, including the hidden sink opening no one will ever see again. Metal edges deburr with a file stroke at 45 degrees each face and a quick pass of emery; plastics wet-sand through grits and, for acrylic, flame-polish or buff to clarity. The habit that binds all of this: inspect the edge in raking light before calling any job done, because raking light is how everyone else will eventually see it.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting: Wander, Bevel Drift, Tearout, Burning, and Breakage
sections.body: Jigsaw faults are few, recurring, and diagnosable, and each has a mechanism worth knowing because the fix follows from it. Cut wanders off line horizontally: either the blade is dull or unevenly set (one side's teeth sharper than the other's pulls the cut sideways — replace it; blades are consumables and a fresh one solves more mysteries than any technique), the feed is too fast for the material, or the operator is steering with side pressure instead of rotation. Cut square on top but beveled or bellied below — the classic hidden fault, discovered only when the pieces part: the flexible blade's free end deflected, from forcing the feed, from a blade too light for the thickness, from a worn guide roller no longer backing the blade, or from turning tighter than the blade's radius so it twisted in the kerf. Fix with a wider, stiffer, sharp blade, slower feed, orbit reduced, roller inspected, and radii respected. Top-face splintering: inherent to up-cutting teeth in veneered or brittle faces; the defensive stack is a fine or reverse-tooth blade, zero orbit, taped and knife-scored line, anti-splinter insert, good face down for standard blades, and slower feed — any one helps, together they nearly eliminate it. Bottom-face breakout instead: back the work with sacrificial scrap. Burning and smoking: the blade is rubbing more than cutting — dull teeth, clogged gullets (too fine a TPI for thick resinous stock), speed too high in a heat-sensitive material, or a pause with the blade spinning in one spot; in a curve, burning localizes exactly where the radius was forced. Blade breakage has three signatures: snapped at the shank means vibration and a loose or bouncing shoe (plant the shoe, clamp the work); snapped mid-body means twisting in a too-tight turn or levering the saw sideways to correct a wander; teeth stripped in a patch means the material won or the pitch was wrong — hitting a hidden screw, or cutting metal with a wood blade. A blade pulled hot from a long cut and instantly plunged into the next warps; let blades cool. Saw judders violently and the cut hammers: fewer than three teeth engaged (pitch too coarse for thin stock — go finer or sandwich the work), or the blade is bottoming out on a support beneath. Motor labors and progress stalls: the kerf is pinching because the offcut sags — support it — or the blade is buried in material beyond its capacity; in deep cuts, retreat a few millimeters periodically to let chips clear. Excessive vibration at the handle with no cut in progress points to a bent blade or a worn plunger bearing; try a new blade first. And the meta-rule that covers the rest: when a cut goes wrong, stop, back out along the kerf, and diagnose — blade, speed, orbit, support, feed, in that order — because continuing a failing cut converts a small blemish into scrap, and every one of these faults costs less to fix at the moment it first appears than one centimeter later.

sections.heading: Maintenance, Blade Economy, and Choosing a Saw
sections.body: A jigsaw asks little care but repays what it gets. After dusty sessions, unplug it and blow or brush debris from the blade clamp, the roller, and the motor vents — packed dust is the usual reason a tool-less clamp stops clicking home, and blocked vents cook motors. Put a drop of light machine oil on the guide roller's pivot occasionally, and inspect the roller's groove: a deep worn channel means the roller has stopped supporting the blade and needs replacement, an inexpensive part on most brands. Check the shoe for burrs (file them off before they scratch a workpiece), verify its squareness to the blade with a small square after any knock or bevel session, and keep the anti-splinter inserts — they are consumables, cheap in packs. On corded saws, inspect the cable where it enters the body, the classic failure point; on cordless, store batteries part-charged and out of frost. Brushed motors eventually need new carbon brushes — sparking and intermittent power are the symptoms, and brushes are a user-replaceable part on most models. Blade economy deserves deliberate policy rather than habit: blades are the cheapest component of every job and the cause of most bad ones, so buy the good ones (bi-metal for anything repeated, ground-tooth for anything visible), buy them in the multi-packs that halve the unit price, sort them in a labeled case rather than a loose drawer that dulls and bends them, and discard without ceremony any blade that is bent, blued from heat, or noticeably slower than new — sharpening jigsaw blades is not economic. A dedicated blade for metal and another for wood, never interchanged, keeps both honest. When choosing or upgrading a saw, rank the features by what actually changes outcomes: low vibration and a solid, slop-free blade guide come first, because they are the difference between a saw that tracks and one that buzzes; then variable speed with electronics that hold speed under load; then orbital settings; then a shoe that locks positively square and adjusts without hunting for a separate key. Stroke length matters for thick stock, and a barrel grip suits low, close curve work while a top handle suits general use — hold both before deciding. Beyond that, an LED, a blower, tool-less shoe tilt, and rail compatibility are conveniences worth having but not paying much for, and raw wattage is nearly irrelevant within the normal range, since technique and blade dominate cutting speed. Corded saws are lighter for their power and never fade mid-job; cordless saws of the current generation cut everything a household asks and add the freedom that makes the jigsaw's go-anywhere character complete — the choice is logistics, not capability. Treated this way, a mid-priced jigsaw is a decades-long tool: the motor outlives fashions, the consumables stay cheap, and the skills — reading a blade, steering a fair curve, opening a clean hole in the middle of a panel — only compound.

guides.safetyNote: Unplug the saw or remove its battery before every blade change or adjustment. Wear safety glasses (chips fly upward toward the face), keep hands and the cord out of the blade path below the work, and check behind installed surfaces for pipes and cables before cutting. Clamp small workpieces rather than hand-holding them, let the blade stop before withdrawing it, and use a fitted respirator plus extraction for MDF and especially fiber-cement dust, which contains crystalline silica.
